Wayback_Machine.title: Wayback Machine
Wayback_Machine.summary: The Wayback Machine is the Internet Archive's collection of saved web pages. It holds more than a trillion captures made since 1996, each one a copy of a page as it stood at a recorded moment, and lets a reader open any of them by URL and date. The item Snapshot of northstar.example (2026) is an example of a single capture.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Crawlers fetch pages and store the bytes with the time of the fetch. A capture is addressed by its original URL and a fourteen-digit timestamp; a request for a date with no capture returns the nearest one. Pages saved on request through Save Page Now are stored the same way as crawled ones and are available within minutes.

sections.heading: Using it
sections.body: Enter a URL to see a calendar of its captures. Choose a date to open that capture. Links inside a saved page point at other captures from the nearest date, so a site can be browsed as it was.

sections.heading: What it does not hold
sections.body: Pages excluded by their owner, pages behind a login and most content loaded by scripts after the page was fetched. A capture is a record of a response, not a working copy of a service.

Software_Library.title: Software Library
Software_Library.summary: The Software Library is the Internet Archive's collection of historical software: shareware, freeware, demos, operating systems and the disk images they came on. Many items run in the browser through an emulator, so a 1990s program can be tried without installing anything. The item Cavern Runner 98 is a shareware game from the collection.
infobox: In-browser (DOS, Windows 3.x, Macintosh, Apple II, arcade)

sections.heading: Scope
sections.body: The library preserves programs as they were distributed: original archives, disk and CD images, documentation, registration cards and the shareware nag screens. Sub-collections cover MS-DOS games, Windows 3.x shareware, classic Macintosh software and console and arcade ROMs contributed by their rights holders.

sections.heading: Emulation
sections.body: Items with an emulator badge run in the browser. The emulator boots a disk image built from the item's files; nothing is downloaded to the reader's machine except the page. Saved states are kept in the browser and are not uploaded.

sections.heading: Contributing
sections.body: Anyone with an account can upload software they have the right to share. Uploads are reviewed for malware and for takedown requests, then added to the appropriate sub-collection.

Live_Music_Archive.title: Live Music Archive
Live_Music_Archive.summary: The Live Music Archive holds audience and soundboard recordings of concerts by artists who permit their live performances to be recorded and shared. It grew from the tape-trading communities of the 1990s and now holds over 250,000 recordings.

sections.heading: Artist policy
sections.body: Only artists who have explicitly allowed taping appear here. An artist can withdraw at any time, in which case their recordings are removed from public access but preserved. Commercial releases are never accepted.

sections.heading: Listening
sections.body: Every recording streams in the browser and downloads in lossless form. Set lists, tapers' notes and recording equipment are recorded per item, and recordings of the same show are grouped so a listener can compare sources.

Open_Library.title: Open Library
Open_Library.summary: Open Library is the Internet Archive's catalogue of books, with one web page for every book ever published as its stated goal. Public-domain works can be read in full; many in-copyright works can be borrowed one reader at a time. The item The Ledger of Ashby Hall is a public-domain novel from the collection.

sections.heading: The catalogue
sections.body: Records come from library catalogues, publishers and readers. Each work has a page collecting its editions; each edition records its publisher, year, pagination and identifiers. Anyone can correct a record.

sections.heading: Reading and borrowing
sections.body: Public-domain books open directly in the reader, page by page, with the scanned page alongside its text. Books still in copyright are lent one copy per reader for one hour or fourteen days, the way a library lends a physical book.

Prelinger_Archives.title: Prelinger Archives
Prelinger_Archives.summary: The Prelinger Archives is a collection of ephemeral films: advertising, educational, industrial and amateur films made between 1927 and the 1980s that were never intended to last. Around 7,000 are available here. The item Our Friend the Transistor is a 1962 educational film from the collection.

sections.heading: What is in it
sections.body: Classroom films, sponsored films made by manufacturers and trade bodies, home movies and civic-education shorts. They record what companies, schools and governments wanted people to think, which makes them a rich record of the ordinary.

sections.heading: Reuse
sections.body: Most films are in the public domain and may be downloaded in the original scan resolution and reused without permission. Items with a known rights holder are marked.

Cavern_Runner_98.title: Cavern Runner 98
Cavern_Runner_98.summary: Cavern Runner 98 is a 1998 shareware platform game for MS-DOS and Windows 95 by the two-person studio Lodestone Software. The shareware release contains the first of three episodes, fifteen levels, and a registration screen asking for 19.95 dollars by post. It runs in the browser through the Software Library's DOS emulator.

sections.heading: About the game
sections.body: The player guides a mine surveyor through flooding caverns, placing lamps to reveal the level and collecting core samples to open the exit. Levels are timed against the rising water. The shareware episode ends with the surveyor reaching the lift shaft and a screen explaining how to order episodes two and three.

sections.heading: Files
sections.body: CAVERN98.ZIP (2.3 MB) contains CAVERN.EXE, the level data, a SETUP.EXE for sound card selection and ORDER.TXT with the postal address. A scan of the registration card is attached as a separate file.

sections.heading: Notes
sections.body: Uploaded from an original shareware CD-ROM compilation. The game requires a Sound Blaster-compatible card for music; the emulator supplies one.

Our_Friend_the_Transistor.title: Our Friend the Transistor
Our_Friend_the_Transistor.summary: Our Friend the Transistor is a 1962 educational film, 16 minutes, produced by Meridian Instructional Films for secondary school science classes. It explains the transistor through a series of demonstrations with an oversized model and compares it, at length, with the vacuum tube it replaces. It is in the public domain.

sections.heading: Synopsis
sections.body: A teacher in a laboratory coat introduces "our friend" and shows what it does: a radio the size of a shoebox becomes one the size of a cigarette packet. The film explains base, emitter and collector with a water-tap model, then visits a factory where transistors are made by hand under microscopes.

sections.heading: About this scan
sections.body: Scanned in 2K from a 16 mm print with faded colour and a scratched first reel. The soundtrack is intact. The print is the only known copy.

The_Midnight_Dispatch.title: The Midnight Dispatch
The_Midnight_Dispatch.summary: The Midnight Dispatch is a radio drama serial broadcast weekly from 1936 to 1939 on a regional network in the American Midwest. Each fifteen-minute episode follows a newspaper night editor who receives a tip the paper cannot print. Forty-one episodes survive from transcription discs and are collected here.

sections.heading: About the serial
sections.body: The serial was sponsored by a coffee brand whose jingle opens every episode. The night editor, Hal Corrigan, was played by the same actor throughout. Episodes are self-contained; the surviving discs are numbered but the numbering has gaps.

sections.heading: About the audio
sections.body: The discs were transferred in 2009 at 96 kHz and are offered here as FLAC and MP3. Surface noise has been reduced lightly; the jingle is unchanged.

The_Ledger_of_Ashby_Hall.title: The Ledger of Ashby Hall
The_Ledger_of_Ashby_Hall.summary: The Ledger of Ashby Hall is an 1899 novel by the English writer Harriet Penrose, out of copyright since 1979. A country house is inherited along with its account books, and the heir reads the ledger back through fifty years to find out where the money went. It is available to read in full or to download.
infobox: Read online, PDF, EPUB, plain text

sections.heading: About the book
sections.body: Penrose's only novel was reviewed well and sold poorly. It was rediscovered in the 1990s and is now taught for its use of accounts as narrative: each chapter opens with a page of the ledger, and the story is what the entries do not say.

sections.heading: About this copy
sections.body: Scanned from the first edition held by a university library. The OCR text has been proofread by volunteers and is complete.

Snapshot_of_northstar.example_(2026).title: Snapshot of northstar.example (2026)
Snapshot_of_northstar.example_(2026).summary: This item is a Wayback Machine capture of the home page of northstar.example, made on 4 February 2026 at 09:14 UTC. The capture is recorded here as an item because it was submitted through Save Page Now with a note, and notes are kept with the item rather than the capture.

sections.heading: Submitter's note
sections.body: Saved before the redesign announced for the following week. The page carries the original product description and the pricing table that was later changed. Kept for reference; nothing on the page is unusual.

sections.heading: What the capture holds
sections.body: The HTML of the home page and the stylesheet it referenced. Images were fetched and stored. A script that loaded the pricing table from a separate endpoint was not executed, so the table appears as it was in the page source.

About.title: About the Internet Archive
About.summary: The Internet Archive is a non-profit digital library founded in 1996 with the mission of universal access to all knowledge. It preserves web pages, software, books, audio and film, and makes them available free of charge to readers, researchers and the public.

sections.heading: Mission
sections.body: Libraries have always kept what was published so that the future could read it. The Internet Archive does the same for what is published digitally, which is to say for most of what is published now.

sections.heading: Collections
sections.body: The Wayback Machine, the Software Library, the Live Music Archive, Open Library and the Prelinger Archives are the largest. Each is linked under See also.

sections.heading: Funding
sections.body: The Archive is funded by donations, grants and library partnerships. It sells nothing and shows no advertising.

Donate.title: Donate
Donate.summary: The Internet Archive is a non-profit. It has no advertising and no paywall, and it keeps its collections available because readers pay for them. A donation of any size supports the servers, the scanning centres and the staff who keep them running.

sections.heading: How to give
sections.body: One-time or monthly gifts are accepted by card, bank transfer and cheque. Donors receive a receipt for tax purposes. Nothing else is sent unless asked for.

sections.heading: Other ways to help
sections.body: Upload material you have the right to share, correct catalogue records in Open Library, or run a mirror. The Archive also accepts donations of physical media for digitisation.

Terms.title: Terms of Use
Terms.summary: These terms govern the use of the Internet Archive's collections. They are short because the collections exist to be used.

sections.heading: Access
sections.body: Reading, listening, viewing and downloading are free. Items may carry their own licences; where an item does, that licence governs reuse. Where it does not, assume the material may be in copyright and act accordingly.

sections.heading: Removal
sections.body: A rights holder may ask for an item to be removed from public access. Removed items are preserved but not served. A site owner may exclude their site from the Wayback Machine.

sections.heading: Conduct
sections.body: Do not use the collections to harass anyone, do not upload material you have no right to share, and do not fetch at a rate that degrades the service for others.
